messages.body_plain:
> On May 28, 2026, at 05:27, Daniel Turek <danie...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Brook, within the past year or so we added a system for monitoring and recording "derived quantities" during an MCMC run.  There are pre-written mechanisms for monitoring:

Yes, that is exactly what I was looking for.

Section 7.2.3 of the NIMBLE manual states the following:

	log-probabilities (log-density values) for single or (summed) groups of nodes

and section 7.2.3.1 states the following:

	Alternatively, the mean, variance, and logProb derived quantities are directly supported
	as arguments to configureMCMC, buildMCMC, and nimbleMCMC.

I have added the following argument to my nimbleMCMC() function call:

	logProb=c(“a_0”, “a_1”)	# these are two of the parameters in the model

The result is that the value generated by nimbleMCMC() includes $derived$logProb, which is a matrix of MCMC samples x parameters, but every value in the matrix is identical.  Nothing changes across samples.

>From the documentation, I expected the sum of ln(P) (not individual values per parameter) and I expected it to change with each sample.

Please explain how I should be doing this, as what seems to be the straightforward interpretation of the documentation is not consistent with what happens.  There must be an (obvious?) catch.

Thanks a lot for your help.

Cheers,
Brook

messages.subject: Re: monitoring posterior probability in nimble
messages.body_plain:
Yes, the documentation attempts to make the following distinction (character vector vs. list), but perhaps it's unclear.

When the logProb argument is provided as a *character vector*, then each element of the character vector has the logProb reported separately:

As in your case:
     logProb=c(“a_0”, “a_1”)     ## character vector; LP for a_0 and a_1 will be reported separately.

When the logProb argument is provided as a *list*, then each element of the list has a logProb reported, which represents the *sum* of the nodes comprising that individual element of the list.

For examples:
    logProb = list("a_0", "a_1")     ## a list, with two elements.  LP for each element, a_0 and a_1 will be reported separately.
    logProb = list(    c("a_0", "a_1")   )     ## a list, with one element (itself a character vector).  the sumed LP for the elements of this list will be reported
    logProb = list(   "x",    "y[1:10]",     c("a", "b", "c")   )     ## a list, with three elements...  3 different LPs will be reported, the second one being the sum for y[1:10], and the third being the summed LPs for nodes a, b, and c.

As for the static values of the LPs you're seeing, I can't address that without seeing a reproducible example.  Hopefully it's not a bug in the derived quantity system itself, although that's never out of the question.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.subject: Re: monitoring posterior probability in nimble
messages.body_plain:
Brook, I'm pleased to report that I believe everything is operating as intended.  Though I see how the results you're seeing appear confusing.

The model you specified, in particular the priors for sigma, a_0, a_1, is:

MCMC_code <- nimbleCode({
    sigma ~ dunif(0,20)
    a_0 ~ dunif(-10,10)
    a_1 ~ dunif(-10,10)
    ...
    ...
})

The priors used for each of sigma, a_0, and a_1 is a uniform distribution, each spanning an interval of width = 20.  No matter what different values each of these nodes attain (so long as they remain within the specified intervals, [0,20] for sigma, and [-10, 10] for the a_0, a_1 terms), the logProb for any of these nodes will be constant, and equal to:

log(1/20) = -2.995732

which explains the value you're seeing.  Using the list syntax, when you *sum* the LP for these three nodes, the value you're seeing is:

log(1/20) + log(1/20) + log(1/20) = -8.987197

When you specify ".all" to sum the LP over *all* stochastic model nodes, this now adds together the logProbs for sigma, a_0, a_1, and each of the 10 y[i] terms.  The LP for each y[i] is a (log) normal density, the value of which depends on the current parameter values, which is why these LP values are changing.  You could verify all the arithmetic, by also recording the LP's for the 10 y[i] terms, verifying those yourself by evaluating the (log) normal density using the different sets of sampled parameter values (in combination with the different x[i] and y[i] values), then finally adding together the 13 different logProb contributions to arrive at the final "_all_nodes_" LP value.

Does this resolve the mystery?

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.subject_clean: How does HMC work with dconstraint?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I saw in the release list that dconstraint now works with HMC. I'm just wondering how this works in practice when the sampler steps outside the constrained region. I saw in the documentation that it says

 "NaN values may be encountered in the course of the leapfrog procedure. In particular, when the stepsize (epsilon) is too large, the leapfrog procedure can step too far and arrive at an invalid region of parameter space, thus generating a NaN value in the likelihood evaluation or in the gradient calculation. These situation are handled by the sampler by rejecting the NaN value, and reducing the stepsize."

Is this like MH, where the current sampled values are set to the previous ones and then the MCMC moves to the next iteration? Or does it keep going and try to find a valid parameter?

Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: How does HMC work with dconstraint?
messages.subject_clean: How does HMC work with dconstraint?
messages.body_plain:
Dirk, this is a good question about how HMC handles stepping out-of-bounds in the parameter space.  No, it's not exactly like the MH accept/reject step, where if a MH sampler proposed value goes "out of bounds," then the proposal is automatically rejected, and the MH sampler proceeds to the next iteration (where it tries a different proposal value).

Rather, the HMC sampler creates trajectories (sequences of locations) through the (possibly multi-dimensional) parameter space.  These trajectories are generated by generating a path approximately following the gradient of the log-likelihood surface, which is done using finite-sized steps (repeatedly calculating the gradient at each location, then taking a small "step" in the direction of the gradient).  Therefore, a (self-tuning) parameter of the HMC sampler is the "stepsize" which is used when generating these trajectories.  In the absence of any out-of-bounds steps, at the conclusion of generating a trajectory (a sequence locations in the parameter space), the HMC sampler selects one of the locations making up the trajectory as the "next sample" - the "next sample" is not necessarily the final location at the terminal end of the trajectory, but rather a random point selected from all locations making up the trajectory, which is selected in a random manner so as to maintain the forward/backward reversible nature of the HMC sampling process, ensuring a reversible Markov chain (as is necessary for valid MCMC sampling).

However, sometimes if the "stepsize" is too large, these finite-sized steps used to generate the trajectory might go out-of-bounds, reaching an invalid location in parameter space.  In that event (in contrast to how the MH sampler operates), the HMC ceases extending the trajectory; some recent part of the trajectory (which itself might be in valid parameter space) may be immediately discarded, as is necessary to ensure reversibility; the "next sample" is selected (still in a random manner) from the remaining part of the trajectory.  And finally, at the next adaptation step (which occurs periodically during the warm-up phase of the HMC sampler), the HMC's internal "stepsize" parameter may be adjusted to be smaller, to help avoid future steps going out-of-bounds.

I hope I've explained this clearly, and it helps answer your question.  You can view the source code the nimble's "NUTS" HMC sampler here <https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimbleHMC/blob/7def926dcff6fdedcea00fb954ebae4a2367911f/nimbleHMC/R/HMC_samplers.R#L807>, although looking at the source code may or may not be elucidating.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a question regarding divergent paths in nimbleHMC. I am running a straightforward regression model that is estimating survival probabilities, by age and sex, with a random intercept of site. I am encountering divergent paths (usually 20-30) in this model. I have increased the "delta" to 0.95 and 0.99 and used non-centered random effects, but there always remains at least 5-10 divergent paths. My question is if there is a way to know if these divergent paths are occurring during warmup or that actual sampling phase? If they are occurring during the warmup period, then are divergent paths an issue?

Thanks,
Jake
